passages.title: Talking Back: Why Screens Cannot Replace Conversation in the Early Years
paragraphs: On a weekday evening in a small apartment in Khon Kaen, a two-year-old sits in front of a tablet while her parents prepare dinner. The cartoon is bright, the songs are catchy, and the child is quiet, which for tired parents can feel like a small victory. Yet a growing body of research suggests that this quiet may come at a cost to the very skill that toddlers are working hardest to acquire: language.

In the first three years of life, language develops largely through what researchers call "conversational turns", the back-and-forth exchanges in which an adult responds to a child's sounds, gestures and first words. A screen, however engaging, cannot respond in this way. A 2022 study of 900 families in northeastern Thailand found that children who spent more than two hours a day with screens produced, on average, 30 percent fewer words at age two than peers whose daily use was under 30 minutes.

The problem lies not only in what children watch but also in what they miss. When a television is left on in the background, parents tend to speak less, and their conversations with children become shorter and simpler. Some researchers have labelled a related pattern "technoference": adults' own phones interrupting moments that would otherwise be filled with talking, singing or reading together.

None of this means that every screen is harmful. Video calls with grandparents, for example, involve genuine turn-taking, and educational programmes watched alongside an adult who names objects and asks questions can support vocabulary growth. What appears to matter most is whether a screen replaces human interaction or becomes a starting point for it.

For parents, the practical message is modest rather than alarming. Paediatricians generally advise avoiding screens, apart from video chatting, before about 18 months, and keeping later use brief and shared. Switching off background television, putting phones away at mealtimes and describing everyday routines aloud are simple, low-cost steps. As Dr. Waraporn Sirisuk, a child development specialist, puts it, "Children do not need perfect parents. They need parents who talk to them."

passages.title: Microlearning: Small Lessons, Big Gains?
paragraphs: Every morning before her shift, a nurse at a district hospital in Udon Thani spends four minutes on her phone answering a single question about hand hygiene. This is microlearning: instruction delivered in brief, focused units, each designed to teach one idea in roughly three to ten minutes. Once linked mainly to corporate training, the approach is now spreading through universities and hospitals, raising an obvious question: can lessons this small produce meaningful learning?

Supporters argue that microlearning suits the way memory works. Because working memory can hold only a little new information at once, short units reduce the risk of overload. More importantly, small lessons are easy to repeat. Research on the spacing effect shows that material reviewed at intervals is remembered far longer than material studied in one long session, and brief quizzes add the benefit of retrieval practice, in which recalling an answer strengthens the memory itself.

Early evidence is encouraging. In a 2023 study at a provincial hospital in northeastern Thailand, 120 nurses learned updated infection-control procedures in one of two ways. Half attended a one-day workshop; the rest completed a five-minute module each working day for six weeks. Three months later, the microlearning group averaged 81 percent on a knowledge test, compared with 67 percent for the workshop group, and followed the procedures more accurately on the ward.

Critics, however, warn against treating microlearning as a cure-all. Complex abilities, such as diagnosing an unusual illness or writing a research proposal, depend on seeing how many pieces of knowledge connect, and such connections are hard to build from isolated fragments. Learners may also mistake familiarity for understanding: finishing dozens of quick quizzes can feel productive even when little deep thinking has occurred.

Many instructional designers therefore describe microlearning as a supplement rather than a substitute. "Short modules are excellent for reinforcing what has already been taught," says Dr. Anucha Phromma, an educational technologist, "but they are weak at introducing ideas that need extended discussion." In practice, this usually means a longer first session followed by short review activities spread over several weeks.

So, can small lessons bring big gains? The evidence suggests a qualified yes: they work best when they are regularly repeated and connected to a larger plan. Used alone, they may produce learners who know many facts but struggle to apply them.

passages.title: Haze Returns to the North as PM2.5 Levels Soar Past Safety Limit
paragraphs: CHIANG MAI — Thick haze blanketed northern Thailand this week as levels of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, stayed above the national safety limit for the twelfth consecutive day. On Tuesday, 11 March, monitoring stations in Mae Hong Son recorded a 24-hour average of 186 micrograms per cubic metre, almost five times the national standard of 37.5 micrograms, which was tightened from 50 micrograms in 2023.

Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai reported averages of 142 and 128 micrograms respectively, while Lampang, usually among the less affected provinces, reached 97. Doctors at a hospital in Chiang Mai said the number of patients treated for asthma and other breathing problems had risen by about 40 percent since the beginning of February.

The smoky season, which typically runs from late January to April, has several causes. Farmers burn crop residue, especially maize stubble, to clear fields before planting, and forest fires spread quickly in the dry heat. Smoke also drifts across the border from neighbouring countries. Geography makes matters worse: Chiang Mai lies in a basin surrounded by mountains, and cool night air can trap pollutants close to the ground until midday.

Satellite data analysed by a research team at a university in northern Thailand detected 2,340 hotspots across the region's nine provinces between 1 and 10 March, compared with 1,860 in the same period last year. More than half were located in forest reserves rather than on farmland, the researchers said.

Provincial authorities have introduced several measures. Open burning is banned until 30 April, with fines of up to 10,000 baht for violators. Government offices have been asked to let staff work from home on days when readings exceed 75 micrograms, and more than 300 schools and health centres have set up "clean rooms" fitted with air purifiers. Free N95 masks are being distributed to pregnant women, young children and older people.

Environmental groups welcomed the steps but said they treated symptoms rather than causes. "Every year we hand out masks, and every year the smoke comes back," said Kittipong Saengthong, coordinator of a local clean-air network. He called for stronger support to help farmers sell crop waste instead of burning it, and for closer cooperation with neighbouring countries.

passages.title: After the Rush: Telemedicine Finds Its Place in Everyday Care
paragraphs: When clinics closed during the COVID-19 pandemic, video consultations went from a niche service to a lifeline almost overnight. Doctors who had never examined a patient through a screen suddenly did so dozens of times a day. Now that waiting rooms are full again, health systems face a quieter but harder question: which parts of this emergency experiment are worth keeping?

The answer, studies suggest, depends heavily on the type of care involved. A 2024 analysis of nearly two million outpatient visits in Southeast Asia found that virtual consultations fell sharply once lockdowns ended, from a peak of 38 percent of all visits to about 9 percent. Even so, that figure was roughly six times higher than before the pandemic, which suggests that telemedicine has settled into a lasting, if limited, role.

That role is clearest in the follow-up of chronic conditions. For a patient with stable diabetes or high blood pressure, a monthly hospital visit can mean a long bus journey, a lost day's wages and hours in a crowded corridor, all for a five-minute conversation and a repeat prescription. Several provincial hospitals in Thailand now offer such patients video appointments instead, with medicines sent by post. Mental health care has moved even further online, since many consultations rely on conversation rather than physical examination.

Yet the technology has clear limitations. A doctor cannot listen to a patient's lungs or feel an abdomen through a phone, and some conditions that look minor on screen prove serious. Dr. Pornthip Chaiyasit, an internal medicine specialist in Khon Kaen, estimates that about one in ten of her virtual patients must still be asked to come in person. "Telemedicine is a useful filter," she says, "but it is not a replacement for the examination room."

Access is another concern. The patients who could benefit most, such as older people in remote villages, are often the least comfortable with smartphones or lack reliable internet. In some districts, village health volunteers now help elderly residents join video calls, an arrangement that bridges the gap but adds to the volunteers' already heavy workload. Questions about data privacy and payment for virtual visits also remain unresolved.

None of these problems is likely to reverse the trend. Most experts instead expect a hybrid model, in which patients see their doctor in person when necessary and online when convenient. The pandemic forced medicine to try something new; the task now is to use it wisely.

passages.title: Teen Sleep Study Points to the Cost of Early Classes
paragraphs: Teachers in many Thai secondary schools know the scene well: a classroom at 8 a.m. in which half the students are struggling to stay awake. A new study suggests that this drowsiness is more than a discipline problem. Researchers at a university in northeastern Thailand surveyed 2,400 students aged 13 to 18 and found that they slept an average of only 6.4 hours on school nights, well below the eight to ten hours generally recommended for this age group. Those who slept less than six hours had grade averages about 0.3 points lower than classmates who slept at least eight.

Part of the explanation lies in biology. During puberty, the body clock shifts later: melatonin, the hormone that signals it is time to sleep, is released one to two hours later than in childhood. Consequently, many teenagers do not feel tired until close to midnight. This is not laziness but a normal stage of development, and it means that a teenager who must wake at 5.30 a.m. is effectively being asked to rise in the middle of his or her biological night.

Lost sleep matters for learning because sleep is when the brain consolidates new information. During deep sleep, memories formed during the day are replayed and transferred to longer-term storage, which is why a night of rest after studying often improves recall the next morning. Sleep-deprived students, by contrast, find it harder to concentrate, remember less of what they are taught and are more likely to report low mood.

In Thailand, social schedules often make the problem worse. Many schools begin with a morning assembly before eight o'clock, and city students may travel an hour or more to get there. In the evenings, many attend private tutoring classes before finishing homework and turning to their phones. In the survey, 58 percent of students said they used a screen in bed after 11 p.m. on most school nights.

Some education systems have responded by starting the school day later. After several school districts in the United States moved high school start times to 8.30 a.m. or later, studies reported longer sleep, better attendance and fewer car accidents among teenage drivers. The Thai researchers argue that even a 30-minute delay, combined with limits on late-evening tutoring, could make a measurable difference. "We cannot change adolescent biology," said the study's lead author, Dr. Nattaya Boonmee, "but we can stop designing school days that work against it."

passages.title: Chatbots in the Classroom: Two Years On
paragraphs: When generative AI chatbots became freely available, many teachers reacted with alarm. Here was a tool that could write a competent essay or solve a page of algebra problems in seconds. Some schools blocked the websites; others hurried to rewrite their assessment rules. Two years on, the debate has shifted: the question is no longer whether students will use these tools, but how they can do so without undermining learning.

For many teachers, chatbots have become a genuinely useful assistant. A secondary teacher in Nakhon Ratchasima, for example, uses one to rewrite the same science article at three levels of difficulty, so that every student in a mixed-ability class can read it. Others generate practice questions, draft rubrics or produce model answers for students to critique. In a 2024 survey of 650 Thai teachers, 61 percent said AI tools saved them at least two hours of preparation a week.

Arthit, a first-year engineering student, submitted an essay on flood management that his lecturer described as almost flawless and quite unlike his earlier assignments. When she invited him to discuss its central argument, however, he could not explain it, and two of the six sources in his bibliography turned out not to exist. A later survey of 800 undergraduates at the same university found that 46 percent had handed in chatbot-generated text as their own at least once, and fewer than a third of them had checked whether the references were real.

Institutions have responded to such cases in very different ways. Some have banned chatbots from assessed work altogether, although enforcement is difficult because detection software is unreliable. Others have redesigned assessment instead, asking students to submit drafts, defend their work orally or complete key tasks in class. A few now require students to declare how they used AI and to evaluate its contribution.

In one Bangkok secondary school, an English teacher asks students to obtain chatbot feedback on a paragraph, decide which suggestions to accept and justify each decision in writing. Down the corridor, a chemistry teacher gives her class a chatbot's explanation of reaction rates containing three deliberate errors for students to find and correct. Both teachers report that their students now question AI output more readily and discuss the subject in greater depth.

Taken together, these experiences suggest that the effect of a chatbot depends less on the technology itself than on the task it is given. Used to replace thinking, it produces polished work and shallow learning; used to provoke thinking, it may become a remarkably powerful study aid.

passages.title: Why Cities Run Hot: The Causes and Costs of Urban Heat Islands
paragraphs: On a hot afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding farmland. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island effect, has been recorded in cities on every inhabited continent. The average difference is often 1 to 3°C, but on calm, clear nights it can exceed 7°C. The effect has several causes, all linked to the way cities are built and used, and it carries significant costs.

The most important cause is the replacement of natural ground cover with artificial surfaces. Asphalt and concrete absorb much of the incoming sunlight and store it as heat. For example, measurements in Bangkok have shown dark roads exceeding 60°C at midday while a nearby grass field stayed below 35°C. Because these materials release stored heat slowly, they keep warming the air after sunset, which is why the temperature gap is often greatest at night.

A second factor is the loss of vegetation. Trees and other plants cool their surroundings through evapotranspiration, the process by which water evaporates from leaves and soil, using energy that would otherwise heat the air. Trees also provide shade. In dense urban districts, however, green space may cover less than a tenth of the land. As a result, much of the sun's energy goes into heating surfaces rather than evaporating water.

The shape of the city also matters. Tall buildings lining narrow streets form what scientists call urban canyons. Sunlight that enters these canyons is reflected from wall to wall instead of escaping back into the sky, and the buildings block winds that could carry heat away. In addition, cities produce waste heat of their own: air-conditioning units, vehicles and factories all release energy into the surrounding air.

These processes have serious consequences. During heatwaves, city residents face a higher risk of heat exhaustion and heatstroke, particularly older people, outdoor workers and those in poorly ventilated housing. Heat also speeds the formation of ground-level ozone, a pollutant that irritates the lungs. Moreover, electricity demand rises as people switch on air conditioners, which release still more waste heat, creating a cycle that is hard to break.

Fortunately, the effect can be reduced. Roofs coated with reflective materials can stay more than 20°C cooler than dark roofs on sunny days. Street trees, parks and green roofs restore some of the cooling lost to development, and permeable pavements hold rainwater that later evaporates and cools the surface. No single measure will eliminate urban heat, but together they can make cities far more liveable.

passages.title: Antibiotic Resistance: A Slow-Moving Crisis
paragraphs: When Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, he opened an era in which infections that had once killed millions became easy to treat. Yet within two decades, Fleming himself was warning that bacteria could learn to survive the drug if it was used carelessly. His warning has proved remarkably accurate. Drug-resistant infections are now estimated to cause more than a million deaths worldwide each year, and the toll is still rising.

Resistance is, in essence, evolution at work. Whenever an antibiotic is used, it kills the susceptible bacteria but may leave behind a few that carry genetic changes allowing them to survive. These survivors multiply and can pass their resistance genes to other bacteria, occasionally even to different species. The more often antibiotics are used, the more opportunities such selection has to occur.

Human behaviour has greatly accelerated this process. Antibiotics are frequently prescribed for colds and sore throats, which are usually caused by viruses and therefore do not respond to antibiotics at all. Patients often keep leftover tablets and take them the next time they feel unwell, and in many countries the drugs can still be bought without a prescription. A 2023 survey of 1,500 adults in three Thai provinces found that 42 percent believed antibiotics could cure the common cold, while a quarter had bought them from a pharmacy without seeing a doctor in the previous year.

Hospitals and farms are two major breeding grounds for resistant bacteria. In the former, seriously ill patients receive powerful antibiotics, and resistant strains can spread between wards on hands and equipment. In the latter, animals have often been given antibiotics not to treat disease but to make them grow faster, a practice that many countries now restrict. Resistant bacteria from livestock can then reach people through food, water and soil.

Meanwhile, very few new antibiotics are reaching the market. Developing one can take more than a decade and cost hundreds of millions of dollars, yet a successful new drug is likely to be held in reserve and used only when older ones fail. This leaves manufacturers with little prospect of recovering their investment, and many large companies have abandoned antibiotic research altogether.

Experts stress that the crisis, though slow-moving, is not inevitable. Stricter infection control in hospitals, rapid tests that show within hours whether an infection is bacterial or viral, tighter rules on farm use and new ways of funding drug development could all slow its progress. Individuals can contribute too, by taking antibiotics only when a health professional prescribes them and exactly as directed.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?

passages.title: Hungry for Knowledge: Food Insecurity Among University Students
paragraphs: University students are often imagined as young people with few responsibilities, living on instant noodles by choice rather than necessity. A growing body of research suggests that this image hides a serious problem. Food insecurity, defined by researchers as a lack of reliable access to enough affordable, nutritious food, is far more prevalent on campuses than many people assume; in several countries it has been found to be as common among students as among low-income families.

In Thailand, a 2024 survey of 3,100 undergraduates at four public universities found that 29 percent had skipped meals or reduced portion sizes at least once a month during the previous semester because they could not afford food. The figure rose to 41 percent among students who were the first in their families to attend university, and to 47 percent among those who received no regular financial support from home.

Many of these students live in precarious circumstances: their income from part-time work is unstable, and a single unexpected expense, such as a medical bill or a broken phone, can leave them unable to buy food for days. Rising rents near campus and the cost of materials for laboratory and studio courses add further pressure.

The consequences extend well beyond hunger. Students who reported food insecurity in the survey had lower average grades, were twice as likely to report symptoms of depression, and were more likely to consider leaving their studies. Researchers point out that the brain needs a steady supply of energy for concentration and memory, so a student who arrives at an 8 a.m. lecture without breakfast is at a genuine disadvantage.

Despite the scale of the problem, few students seek help. Many are deterred by stigma, the sense of shame and social disapproval attached to admitting that one cannot afford to eat. Others simply do not know that support exists. "Students tell us they would rather go hungry than be seen collecting free food," says Dr. Kanokwan Rattanapong, a sociologist who worked on the study.

Some universities have begun to respond. Campus food banks now distribute staples such as rice, eggs, cooking oil and canned fish, and several faculties offer meal vouchers that can be used discreetly at ordinary canteens. Researchers welcome these efforts but warn that help has so far been sporadic rather than regular and predictable, often depending on donations that arrive in some months and not in others. Lasting solutions, they argue, will require food support to be built into university welfare policies.

passages.title: From Waste to Resource: Plastics and the Circular Economy
paragraphs: Plastic is one of the defining materials of modern life: light, durable and cheap, it has become indispensable in packaging, medicine and construction. Global production now exceeds 400 million tonnes a year, yet the model behind this output remains largely linear: resources are extracted, made into products, used, often only once, and discarded. Less than a tenth of all plastic waste ever generated has been recycled; the rest has been burned, buried or allowed to leak into rivers and oceans. This article examines whether a circular economy offers a realistic alternative, and what stands in its way.

In a circular economy, materials are kept in use for as long as possible, and waste is treated as a design flaw rather than an unavoidable outcome. Advocates usually describe a hierarchy of strategies. The most desirable is to reduce the amount of plastic used in the first place, for instance by eliminating unnecessary packaging. Next comes reuse, such as refillable bottles and containers. Recycling, which turns used plastic into raw material for new products, ranks below both, because it consumes energy and usually degrades the material. Disposal is the last resort.

Recycling nevertheless remains the most visible element of circular policies, and its performance has been disappointing. Several technical obstacles explain this. Many products combine different polymers, or layers of plastic and aluminium, which cannot easily be separated. Food residue and labels contaminate collected material, lowering its value. Even clean plastic loses quality each time it is melted, so a drinks bottle may become a fibre for clothing but rarely another bottle. Economics compounds these problems: when oil prices are low, new or "virgin" plastic is often cheaper than recycled plastic, leaving recyclers with little demand for their output.

In many developing countries, the gap left by weak formal systems is partly filled by informal workers. In Thailand, people known locally as saleng travel through neighbourhoods on motorcycle carts, buying bottles, cans and cardboard from households and selling them to scrap dealers. Community waste banks have built on this tradition. In one district of Khon Kaen, residents deposit sorted recyclables at a monthly collection point and receive credit that can be used for small loans or funeral funds; organisers report that the amount of waste sent to the local landfill fell by about a quarter in the scheme's first three years.

Governments have several tools for strengthening such efforts. Under extended producer responsibility (EPR), companies that sell packaged goods must pay for the collection and recycling of their packaging, which gives them a financial reason to design products that are easier to recycle. Deposit-return schemes add a small refundable charge to each bottle or can; some European schemes now recover more than 90 percent of the containers sold. Other measures include minimum recycled-content requirements for new products and bans on items that are hard to recycle, such as certain single-use plastics.

Critics caution, however, that the circular economy can be invoked to justify business as usual. If recycling is presented as the solution, they argue, companies may feel free to keep increasing production, even though most plastic still escapes collection. Chemical recycling, which breaks plastics down into basic molecules, is promoted as a way to handle mixed waste, but it is energy-intensive and has so far operated only on a relatively small scale. International negotiations on a global plastics agreement, launched in 2022, have exposed deep disagreement over whether production itself should be capped.

The evidence therefore suggests that a circular economy for plastics is achievable only in part, and only if recycling is treated as one tool among several rather than the centrepiece. Reducing unnecessary use, designing products for reuse and repair, making producers responsible for their waste and supporting the people who already collect it must proceed together. The goal is not simply to manage waste more efficiently, but to stop treating valuable materials as waste in the first place.
